claims.text: A tailored nanostructure of magnetically active clusters primarily governs the strong low-field magnetocaloric response in rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys.
Inherent chemical disorder promotes the formation of magnetically active nanoclusters.
Magnetically active clusters create a broad distribution of local exchange interactions.
The distribution of local exchange interactions enables rapid magnetic reorientation at low applied fields.
Rapid low-field magnetic reorientation produces a significant magnetic entropy change.
The nanoclusters facilitate efficient heat exchange.
The nanocluster structure reduces magnetic hysteresis without compromising mechanical stability.
The initial as-cast alloy is chemically disordered and lacks a deliberately introduced nanostructured magnetic phase.
Controlled thermal annealing can induce a more uniform and refined distribution of nanoscale magnetic clusters without changing overall composition or macroscopic phase stability.
Cluster density, size, and distribution uniformity mediate local exchange interactions.
Annealing modifies local atomic arrangements and promotes nanoscale clusters having a range of exchange strengths.
The clusters collectively reorient under applied field with low coercivity.
Distributed magnetic reversal minimizes hysteresis while sustaining efficient heat transfer and mechanical robustness.
Relative to the as-cast baseline, the annealed sample will exhibit a larger low-field magnetic entropy change.
Relative to the as-cast baseline, the annealed sample will exhibit reduced magnetic hysteresis.
Relative to the as-cast baseline, the annealed sample will maintain or improve mechanical stability.
The relative magnetocaloric improvement may be on the order of tens of percent.
The proposed effect should be most pronounced near the magnetic transition temperature at applied fields up to approximately 1 T.
Extreme chemical disorder that completely suppresses local magnetic ordering limits the proposed effect.
